points: Draw solution salinity 35 grams per litre and feed salinity 0.5 grams per litre for the tested pair.
Peak power density 4.8 watts per square metre at an applied pressure of 12 bar.
Spread of the peak power density: standard deviation 0.3 watts per square metre across 3 membrane modules.
Baseline first-generation membrane in the same cell: 3.1 watts per square metre at the same applied pressure.
Water flux at the peak: 18 litres per square metre per hour.
Pumping and pretreatment load 0.9 watts per square metre, giving a net power density of 3.9 watts per square metre.
definitions: PRO = pressure-retarded osmosis, power generation at a membrane from a salinity difference
power density = net electric power divided by membrane area, in watts per square metre
draw solution = the concentrated stream that receives permeating water across the membrane
feed = the dilute stream that supplies permeating water
limits: The peak value holds at 25 degrees Celsius, and operation beyond 72 hours was not tested.
prose:
Pressure-retarded osmosis (PRO), power generation at a membrane from a salinity difference, produces power where feed water permeates into a pressurised draw solution, the concentrated stream that receives permeating water across the membrane. Power density, the net electric power divided by membrane area, sets the membrane area a plant requires for a stated output. The draw solution carried a salinity of 35 grams per litre and the feed, the dilute stream that supplies permeating water, carried 0.5 grams per litre. Peak power density reached 4.8 watts per square metre (standard deviation 0.3 watts per square metre across 3 membrane modules) at an applied pressure of 12 bar. A first-generation membrane in the same cell gave a baseline of 3.1 watts per square metre at the same applied pressure. The selective layer in both membranes was polyamide on a porous support, and feed and draw streams ran in countercurrent flow throughout each run. Pressure was raised in steps, and each step was held until the flux reading settled. Membranes from the same casting batch served in every module, and gasket leakage was checked before each run. A concentration polarisation layer formed at the membrane surface during each run, and stirring at the feed side held that layer thin during the peak readings.

Water flux at the peak reached 18 litres per square metre per hour, and flux at each pressure step was recorded after the reading stabilised. Pumping and pretreatment loads consumed 0.9 watts per square metre, and net power density was 3.9 watts per square metre. The gap between gross and net output matches the measured pumping load, and no further loss term was required to close the power balance for the tested pair. The peak value holds at 25 degrees Celsius, and operation beyond 72 hours was not tested. Fouling behaviour, cleaning recovery, and membrane ageing sit outside the tested window, and the reported densities carry no allowance for any of the three.

points: Viscosity of the reference slag at 1500 degrees Celsius: 0.42 pascal seconds.
Viscosity of the same slag at 1450 degrees Celsius: 0.61 pascal seconds, a rise of 45 percent against the higher temperature value.
Basicity, the mass ratio of calcium oxide to silicon dioxide, held at 1.2 for the temperature pair.
Raising basicity to 1.6 at the higher temperature lowered viscosity below the reference value.
Alumina content compared at 12 percent by mass and at 18 percent by mass.
Spread of repeated viscosity readings: standard deviation 0.03 pascal seconds over 4 slag compositions.
Measurement by rotating cylinder at 60 revolutions per minute under a nitrogen cover gas.
definitions: viscosity = resistance of the molten slag to flow, in pascal seconds
basicity = mass ratio of calcium oxide to silicon dioxide in the slag
slag = the molten oxide layer that covers liquid steel in the furnace
limits: Readings cover the stated temperature interval only, and crystallisation below the interval was not characterised.
prose:
Slag, the molten oxide layer that covers liquid steel in the furnace, controls metal droplet settling and refining rates through slag viscosity, the resistance of the molten slag to flow. Viscosity was measured with a rotating cylinder at 60 revolutions per minute under a nitrogen cover gas, and each reported value is a mean over repeated readings with a standard deviation of 0.03 pascal seconds across 4 slag compositions. The reference slag, at a basicity of 1.2, gave a viscosity of 0.42 pascal seconds at 1500 degrees Celsius. Basicity is the mass ratio of calcium oxide to silicon dioxide in the slag. The same slag at 1450 degrees Celsius gave 0.61 pascal seconds, a rise of 45 percent against the higher temperature value. A furnace that loses the stated temperature interval faces the higher viscosity in tapping and in droplet separation, and the measured rise sets the size of that penalty.

Composition moved viscosity in the opposite direction. Raising basicity to 1.6 at the higher temperature lowered viscosity below the reference value, and the decrease was recorded at both alumina contents in the comparison, 12 percent by mass and 18 percent by mass. Alumina raised viscosity at each basicity, and the alumina effect was smaller at the higher basicity. Readings cover the stated temperature interval only, and crystallisation below the interval was not characterised. Plant slags with suspended solids fall outside the tested compositions, and the reported values carry no correction for a solid fraction. The crucible held each sample clear of the furnace wall, and temperature was read by a thermocouple beside the sample rather than from the furnace controller. Cooling was carried out under the same cover gas, and each sample was sectioned after cooling for a check on crystals at the surface. Viscosity ordering across the tested compositions matched the ordering from a falling-ball check in the same furnace, and the falling-ball route confirms the rotating cylinder readings by an independent method.

points: Feedstock mass per windrow: 850 kilograms, at an initial moisture content of 58 percent by mass.
Peak windrow temperature 63 degrees Celsius, reached on day 6.
Temperature held at or above 55 degrees Celsius for 9 days.
Ambient temperature during the trial averaged 21 degrees Celsius.
Carbon to nitrogen ratio of the feedstock mix: 28.
Windrows turned every 4 days.
Indicator bacteria reduction over the trial: 3.2 log units.
Final moisture content 41 percent by mass at day 30, with a final core temperature of 38 degrees Celsius.
Spread of peak temperature: standard deviation 1.8 degrees Celsius across 3 replicate windrows.
definitions: windrow = a long pile of composting material, turned mechanically to supply air
log unit = a tenfold change in a counted quantity
thermophilic range = the temperature band in which heat-loving microorganisms dominate the decomposition
limits: The profile covers one feedstock mix at the stated ratio, and winter operation at lower ambient temperature was not tested.
prose:
Windrow temperature governs pathogen destruction and decomposition rate in composting, and a windrow, a long pile of composting material turned mechanically to supply air, exposes the temperature history of the whole pile in a single core reading. Each windrow held 850 kilograms of feedstock at an initial moisture content of 58 percent by mass and a carbon to nitrogen ratio of 28. Peak core temperature reached 63 degrees Celsius (standard deviation 1.8 degrees Celsius across 3 replicate windrows) on day 6. Temperature held at or above 55 degrees Celsius, the lower edge of the thermophilic range in which heat-loving microorganisms dominate the decomposition, for 9 days. Ambient temperature during the trial averaged 21 degrees Celsius, and the windrows were turned every 4 days.

Indicator bacteria fell by 3.2 log units over the trial, a log unit being a tenfold change in a counted quantity, and the reduction was recorded in samples from the windrow core at the end of the hot period. Final moisture content was 41 percent by mass at day 30, with a final core temperature of 38 degrees Celsius. The temperature record and the bacteria record cover the same window, and the reduction sits inside the period the pile spent in the thermophilic range. The profile covers one feedstock mix at the stated ratio, and winter operation at lower ambient temperature was not tested. Feedstocks with a woody fraction, and piles built at a larger scale, fall outside the tested conditions. Core temperature was read at the centre of each windrow, and shoulder readings tracked the core reading through the hot period. Moisture was checked at each turning, and water was added at turning when the surface layer dried. The feedstock was a mix of green waste, straw, and screened overs from an earlier batch, shredded before the windrows were built. Decomposition in the shoulder layer lagged the core, and turning moved shoulder material into the core at each pass.

points: Worked example goal: reduce the pressure drop relation for pipe flow to dimensionless groups and evaluate both groups, 2 in total, for a stated case.
The relation carries 5 variables: pressure drop, density, velocity, diameter, and viscosity.
The variables span 3 fundamental dimensions: mass, length, and time.
The variable count minus the dimension count gives 2 independent dimensionless groups.
Case inputs: density 998 kilograms per cubic metre, velocity 1.5 metres per second, diameter 0.05 metres, viscosity 0.001 pascal seconds, pressure drop 3200 pascals.
Reynolds number from the case inputs: 74850.
The velocity squared in the pressure group: 2.25 square metres per square second.
Pressure group value from the case inputs: 1.43.
definitions: dimensionless group = a product of variables in which the fundamental dimensions cancel
Reynolds number = density times velocity times diameter, divided by viscosity, a ratio of inertial to viscous effects
pressure group = pressure drop divided by density times velocity squared
fundamental dimension = a base quantity, mass, length, or time, from which the units of a variable are built
prose:
A dimensionless group is a product of variables in which the fundamental dimensions cancel, and a relation written in dimensionless groups holds at any scale that shares the group values. The goal in this tutorial is a reduction of the pressure drop relation for pipe flow to 2 independent dimensionless groups, with both groups evaluated for a stated case. The reader needs a unit check for each variable before the reduction starts. The Buckingham Pi method counts variables, counts the fundamental dimensions the variables span, and subtracts the second count from the first. A fundamental dimension is a base quantity, mass, length, or time, from which the units of a variable are built.

The worked example takes pressure drop in a horizontal pipe as the quantity of interest. Inputs are 5 variables: pressure drop, density, velocity, diameter, and viscosity. The variables span 3 fundamental dimensions, and the subtraction gives the 2 groups. One group is the Reynolds number, density times velocity times diameter divided by viscosity, a ratio of inertial to viscous effects. The second group is the pressure group, pressure drop divided by density times velocity squared. Case inputs are a density of 998 kilograms per cubic metre, a velocity of 1.5 metres per second, a diameter of 0.05 metres, a viscosity of 0.001 pascal seconds, and a pressure drop of 3200 pascals. The Reynolds number from the case inputs is 74850. Velocity squared is 2.25 square metres per square second, and the pressure group from the case inputs is 1.43. The result shows a flow deep in the turbulent range, and a second pipe at the same Reynolds number and the same pressure group reproduces the case behaviour at a different diameter. A reader check repeats the subtraction and the two group evaluations from the stated inputs, and a mismatch at any step locates the error before the groups are used. The method needs no property table beyond the units of the variables already in the relation.

points: Worked example goal: track the liquid level in a draining tank after a step change in inflow, and state the level at one time constant.
Tank cross-sectional area: 2 square metres, constant with height.
Inflow after the step: 0.03 cubic metres per second.
Outflow relation: outflow rate equals the level multiplied by a coefficient of 0.01 per second.
Initial level: 1.2 metres.
Steady level, from inflow divided by the outflow coefficient: 3 metres.
Time constant, from area divided by the outflow coefficient: 200 seconds.
Initial gap between steady level and initial level: 1.8 metres.
Gap factor at one time constant: 0.368, giving a remaining gap of 0.66 metres.
Level at one time constant: 2.34 metres.
definitions: level = height of liquid in the tank, in metres
steady level = the level at which outflow equals inflow and the level stops changing
time constant = the time for the gap between the level and the steady level to fall to the stated fraction of its initial value
mass balance = accumulation equals inflow minus outflow for the tank contents
prose:
A mass balance, accumulation equals inflow minus outflow for the tank contents, tracks a liquid level after a disturbance without a simulation. The goal in this tutorial is the level history of a draining tank after a step change in inflow, with the level stated at one time constant. The reader needs the outflow relation and the tank area before the calculation starts. A warning stands at the first step: the outflow coefficient carries units of per second, and a coefficient taken from a chart in other units corrupts every later value.

The worked example takes a vertical tank with a cross-sectional area of 2 square metres, constant with height. Inputs are an inflow after the step of 0.03 cubic metres per second, an outflow relation in which the outflow rate equals the level multiplied by a coefficient of 0.01 per second, and an initial level of 1.2 metres. Level is the height of liquid in the tank. The steady level, the level at which outflow equals inflow and the level stops changing, is 3 metres from the inflow divided by the outflow coefficient. The time constant, the time for the gap between the level and the steady level to fall to the stated fraction of its initial value, is 200 seconds from the area divided by the outflow coefficient. The initial gap between the steady level and the initial level is 1.8 metres. At one time constant the remaining gap is the initial gap multiplied by 0.368, a remaining gap of 0.66 metres, and the level at one time constant is 2.34 metres. The result shows a level that closes most of the stated gap early and approaches the steady level in steps of the same fraction. A reader check repeats the two divisions and the final multiplication from the stated inputs; any level past the steady level signals an arithmetic error, since the approach is monotone. The same construction serves for a falling level after a downward step in inflow.

points: Emission peak of the film: 530 nanometres, with a full width at half maximum of 28 nanometres.
Quantum yield of the film: 91 percent, standard deviation 2 percentage points across replicate films.
Quantum yield of the baseline polymer film: 74 percent.
Film thickness: 12 micrometres.
Colour gamut coverage: 118 percent of the standard red green blue space.
Brightness retention: 96 percent of the initial value after 500 hours of continuous operation.
definitions: quantum dot = a semiconductor crystal small enough for its size to set the emitted wavelength
quantum yield = photons emitted divided by photons absorbed, as a percentage
full width at half maximum = the wavelength interval across which emission stays at or above half the peak value
sRGB = the standard red green blue colour space used for display specification
prose: Display films based on a quantum dot, a semiconductor crystal small enough for its size to set the emitted wavelength, convert backlight into narrow-band colour, and conversion efficiency sets the brightness a display reaches at a stated backlight power. A film with cadmium-free quantum dots in a barrier-coated polymer matrix was prepared by slot-die coating and characterised against a baseline polymer film. Emission from the film was narrow and centred in the green. The emission peak stood at 530 nanometres with a full width at half maximum, the wavelength interval across which emission stays at or above half the peak value, of 28 nanometres. Quantum yield, photons emitted divided by photons absorbed, reached 91 percent (standard deviation 2 percentage points across replicate films), against 74 percent for the baseline polymer film. Film thickness was 12 micrometres, colour gamut coverage was 118 percent of sRGB, the standard red green blue colour space used for display specification, and brightness retention was 96 percent of the initial value after 500 hours of continuous operation. A yield at the stated level with a narrow emission band supports backlight units with a thinner conversion layer.

points: Crop cycle for the leafy greens in the study system: 28 days from transplant to harvest.
Reported nitrate swing under timed dosing in production systems: from 3 to 14 millimoles per litre within one cycle.
Reported water use under timed dosing: 6.4 litres per kilogram of harvested produce.
Water use reported for closed-loop recirculation: 1.9 litres per kilogram of harvested produce.
Control set point in the planned study: electrical conductivity held at 1.8 decisiemens per metre.
Planned trial duration: 12 weeks of continuous operation.
definitions: nutrient solution = the waterborne feed that carries dissolved mineral nutrients to the roots
EC = electrical conductivity, a measure of the total dissolved salt content of the solution
hydroponic = grown with roots in a nutrient solution rather than in soil
prose: Vertical farms grow leafy greens in stacked hydroponic layers, hydroponic meaning grown with roots in a nutrient solution rather than in soil, under electric lighting with a crop cycle of 28 days from transplant to harvest. The nutrient solution, the waterborne feed that carries dissolved mineral nutrients to the roots, sets growth rate and leaf quality in every layer. Timed dosing is the established control practice in production systems. Reported nitrate concentration under timed dosing swings from 3 to 14 millimoles per litre within one cycle, and reported water use under timed dosing is 6.4 litres per kilogram of harvested produce. Closed-loop recirculation cuts the water figure, with 1.9 litres per kilogram reported for recirculating systems. Whether a constant solution composition, held by continuous sensing and dosing, removes the growth variation that the nitrate swing produces is missing knowledge: published trials vary dosing schedules, and composition in those trials moves with the schedule. The study described here holds EC, electrical conductivity, a measure of the total dissolved salt content of the solution, at a set point of 1.8 decisiemens per metre for 12 weeks of continuous operation, with nitrate, potassium, and calcium each sensed and dosed on a separate loop. Growth uniformity, water use, and leaf nitrate content are the recorded responses. Leaf shape and colour are scored at harvest on a fixed grading scale, applied by the same assessor across layers.

points: Array size: 3 turbines, each rated at 500 kilowatts.
Trial duration: 8 months of continuous operation at one site.
Array capacity factor: 31 percent, standard deviation 4 percentage points across months.
Single-turbine baseline capacity factor at the same site: 34 percent.
Energy generated by the array of 3 turbines over the trial: 2.7 gigawatt hours.
Turbine spacing in the array: 5 rotor diameters.
Array availability: 94 percent of the trial period.
Tidal range at the site: up to 6 metres.
definitions: capacity factor = energy generated divided by the energy the array would generate at continuous rated output, over the same period
wake = the slowed flow downstream of a turbine rotor
availability = the share of a period in which a turbine stands ready to generate
limits: The trial covers one site with a tidal range up to the stated value, and a full annual cycle of biofouling growth was not covered.
prose: The array trial supports a bounded claim: a 3 turbine array at 5 rotor diameters spacing delivers a capacity factor near the single-turbine value at the same site, at the tested site conditions, with array interaction as the measured penalty. Capacity factor, energy generated divided by the energy the array would generate at continuous rated output over the same period, was 31 percent (standard deviation 4 percentage points across months) for the array, against 34 percent for the single-turbine baseline. The array, 3 turbines each rated at 500 kilowatts, generated 2.7 gigawatt hours over 8 months of continuous operation. Availability, the share of a period in which a turbine stands ready to generate, was 94 percent of the trial period, and availability losses and wake losses, the wake being the slowed flow downstream of a turbine rotor, account for the full gap between the array value and the baseline. Two evidence strands combine in the claim: the generation record sets the capacity factor, and the availability record separates downtime from flow interaction. The claim carries its limits. The trial covers one site with a tidal range up to 6 metres, and a full annual cycle of biofouling growth was not covered. Spacing below the tested value, and sites with a stronger directional spread in the flow, sit outside the tested scope. Maintenance visits were grouped into neap-tide windows, and no visit required a rotor lift during the trial. Marine growth on the blades was photographed at each visit and graded against the same photographic scale.
